That thing was over and done.
Toshizō had turned his back on Osae and settled himself again. Behind him, Osae seemed to be putting her dress to rights.
(Too hollow. …)
Toshizō dropped his eyes to the yellowed matting. Toward himself he felt something past all bearing.
(Contemptible.)
Himself, he meant.
For all that he had met again with Osae of the Saruwatari, to hurry a coupling on torn matting like this—what a chill, sorry thing it was.

Once, Toshizō had yearned after love-affairs of splendor. An affair, he had thought, must be a thing of splendor. Always, in Bushū, he had loved the daughters of good blood. Osae had been one of them.
And now those two had met again in Kyoto, and this tryst was no better than the rutting of a farmhand in a stable.
Osae, too, was wretched. Taking Toshizō's weight upon her almost as one taken by force, Osae must have felt her own wretchedness.
In one instant the past had faded.
(To keep the finery of the past from fading, I ought to have made ready some other place, and met her there.)
The past, he thought, called for just that much caution and cunning.
(There is no pleasure in it.)
His heart had only grown wretched, and that was all.
Toshizō drew the small blade from his short sword and began to pare his nails. If he could, he had an urge to drive it through a finger and draw blood.
"Hijikata-sama."
Osae looked back over her shoulder.

She had come to call him by that name. The newer impression—not Toshi the medicine-peddler of Ishida in Hino-juku of Bushū, but the vice-commander of the Shinsengumi who set Kyoto trembling—must lie the darker in Osae's eyes.
"What is it?"
"You have changed, haven't you."
She said it with a touch of scorn. Osae, too, must have felt a keen disappointment.
"I don't take myself to have changed."
"No—like another man altogether."
Osae smoothed back a loose strand of hair.
"Where have I changed?"
"In the whole of you."
"Say it so I can understand."
"In those days, our love-play was merry, like puppies tumbling together. You too, Hijikata-sama—no, Toshi-san—were innocent as a puppy. Now it is otherwise."
"Where?"
Osae could not have said. Nor could Toshizō.
(And yet, come to think of it—)
Toshizō pared off a single nail-paring.

(Once, I yearned after Osae's rank. That turned into my whole manner, and to Osae, I suppose, it looked fresh and green. But now my standing is not what it was. A mere country Shintō priest's daughter of Bushū—I have stopped taking her for good blood. Just so: I have changed. And perhaps it is a very great change indeed.)
Again he pared off a nail.
(It was a fool's business. The past is a thing to be remembered, not a thing to be embraced.)
"You have changed too."
"To the eyes of a Hijikata-sama grown into another man, no doubt I look changed; but Osae is just as she was of old."
(No.)

Osae had plainly become another woman. To begin with, she said she was in service at a court noble's mansion, yet her dress was in the old samurai style, the hem of her kimono grimed, and there was about her the look of a life worn down.
"Are you truly in the service of the Kujō house?"
"Yes."
"That's a lie, surely."
Osae went white in the face of a sudden.
(A lie past doubt. True enough, she went up to Kyoto meaning to serve the Kujō, and serve them she likely did. But for some reason she has left her master's house and lives now in the town.)
Toshizō shifted the small blade to his left hand, to cut the nails of his right.
(I would rather not think it, but—)
Toshizō set the edge of the blade to his thumbnail and bore down hard. The nail split and flew.
(The Lady Osae's body has changed. She has a husband, or a lover, past doubt. And by the look of her, her living is none too easy.)
Toshizō looked at Osae.
"Your husband—is he not a Chōshū man?"
The color changed in Osae's face.
"Better we had not met."
Toshizō laughed.
"Today's business I shall forget.—And you, Osae,"
forget it too, he said, and rose. It might be a man's selfishness, but Toshizō did not want the image he carried within him, the image of the Saruwatari daughter of old, to be broken.
He slid the screen shut and stepped down to the earthen floor.
As he was feeling for his sandals in the dark, of a sudden he sensed someone out toward the front. A neighbor, perhaps, he thought; but out of habit he had no wish to step straight out into the road.
He cut through to the back, opened the rear wicket, and went out. Here there was no one.

(It may be that some bad string is tied to her. She was in service at a court noble's mansion, after all. Loyalist rōnin by the crowd must have come and gone there. Since the regent Kujō fell and withdrew to Kujō village south of the city, Osae may have taken up with one of those loyalist rōnin.)
Toshizō set off westward along Ayanokōji. He meant to go out as far as the gate of the Bukkō-ji and there call for a palanquin.
(What sort of lover, I wonder.)
Toshizō walked. There was a jealousy in him that ached, but with his back teeth he crushed it desperately down.

Of course Toshizō, careless as he was, had not the least inkling just then that the woman he had once coupled with was now a heroine among the loyalist rōnin, a woman of parts who had made a name for her wit.
Saruwatari Osae.
Once a senior waiting-woman of the Kujō house.
Now she lived in an old house behind the Great Buddha, once the country retreat of the abbess-princess of the Hōkyō-ji, and taught the science of poetry.

That was the face of it; but this retreat was one of the hiding-places of samurai who had fled their several clans. Osae, in sympathy with their thinking, kept the old house and looked after them, and had become a sort of loyalist heroine. In that time she had changed men more than once. There had been a Tosa clansman. There had been a Chōshū clansman. And then again a "man of high purpose" no better than a ruffian, whose home province was not even certain. Each time she changed men, the mark they left in Osae grew deeper.

Osae had, too, the backing of her old master the Kujō house. Thanks to her mansion service, she had a face among the court nobility. When the rōnin wished to meet a court noble, she took the trouble to broker it. Naturally she came to be prized among the rōnin.

Osae was content with her present lot. Were she to go home to the Saruwatari in her province, it was already her brother's generation, and there was no place for a sister come back divorced to sit. Better Kyoto than that. Each day here had a spring to it.
(Osae has changed.)
Toshizō went into the Yoshikago by the gate of the Bukkō-ji and ordered a palanquin.
The master of the Yoshikago knew Toshizō's face.
"Ah—"

and, all deference, he sent a young hand running to Gion. In Edo one is never at a loss for a town palanquin, but in Kyoto they are kept standing by only near the pleasure quarters. Even a house the size of the Yoshikago had not one on the premises after dark.
In the meantime there was time and to spare.
Toshizō sat down on the doorframe. In the Yoshikago even the wife, her face gone dead pale with strain, waited on him with tea.
"It's a poor place, but will you not step up to the inner room?"
"No matter."
Toshizō, in this man's way of his, said it curtly. His face gave no purchase to lay hold of.
"But then, sir—"

and the couple fretted and dithered. In its early days, in Serizawa's time, the Shinsengumi had been feared by the townsfolk simply for its violence; but of late a certain formal weight had settled heavily upon it, the standing of a body placed under the Protector of Kyoto. And to say the vice-commander of that body was to name a man of the first rank in the Kyoto of the day. And yet Toshizō was a man forever inside the barracks, who kept up no acquaintance whatever with the clans. In the town even a child knew the name of Hijikata Toshizō, vice-commander of the Shinsengumi, but few had seen his face or his figure. That gloomy, ungracious impression only spread his name through the town the more, a name to make men shudder.
The Yoshikago couple's flustering, too, must come of that same preconception.
After a long while, Toshizō spoke at last.
"Master—forgive me, but,"
his eyes stayed fixed on the street through the dark earthen-floored passage.
"someone seems to be watching your shop."
"Eh!"

"There's nothing to be startled at. It seems there's a man who has followed me here. Forgive me, but might I trouble the mistress? Would she walk out along the front road a chō or so and see how things stand?"
"Er—"
the master's face went timid.
But in a matter of this kind, it seems it is the woman whose nerve holds. The Yoshikago wife, the shaved arches of her brows a fresh blue-black,
"I'll go and look,"
and went out with a paper lantern.
Presently she came back.
"Two at the corner of Takeyamachi. Three at the corner of Nijōhanjiki-chō—rōnin, it seems, that I don't know the look of."
"Five."
"Aye."
"Rather too many."
Toshizō gave a small laugh.

The wife, drawn in despite herself, laughed too, showing her lovely blackened teeth. She seemed to be taking a liking to Toshizō. She had thought the vice-commander of the Shinsengumi some devil of a man, and here, past all expectation, he had clean double-folded eyelids and a cool look about the eyes.
"Hijikata-sensei—if you like, shall I have one of our young men run to Mibu for you?"
She meant, call for reinforcements. The master gave his wife's sleeve a quiet tug.
(Leave it.)
That was his signal, no doubt. Let it be known they had shown the Shinsengumi a kindness, and there was no telling what reprisal the rōnin might visit on them later.
"No matter."
Toshizō went back to his ungracious look.
Before long the palanquin came.
This kind, with a hanging screen, they call in Edo a yotsude-kago; in Kyoto they call it a yotsuji-kago. The shape is much alike.
"Master, a lively-looking young fellow."
"Aye—he's a Tanba man, you see."
"Are Tanba men lively?"
"Well, so they say in the Kamigata."
"That is a comfort."
Toshizō drew a bit of silver from his breast and gave it to the young hand.
"So much!"
"No—take it. Now then: I go home on foot."
"Eh?"
In the earthen passage they were all dumbfounded.
"But I have a favor to ask. In my stead, will you fill that cask there with water and carry it to the Kamo River?"
"Sir.—"
the master of the Yoshikago seemed to read the contrivance Toshizō had drawn in his head.
"That would be awkward for us."

Two rōnin were posted at the corner of Takeyamachi. They would take the palanquin with its cask for the vice-commander of the Shinsengumi and fall on it. The young man would throw the palanquin down and run, and so come to little harm. But afterward it was the master who would have the rough rōnin at his back for helping in such a trick.
The mistress understood Toshizō's plan too. But she took a line other than her husband's.
"Yasu, Shichi—get the cask ready at once. Carry it heavy, mind, as though there were a person aboard."
"Eh—"
the Tanba men drew the palanquin into the passage, made the water-cask ready, and presently,
"Up she comes!"
and hoisted it. Seventeen or eighteen kan, by the look of it.
The palanquin went out. Eastward.

Directly after, Toshizō slipped out from under the eaves and turned the opposite way, west. He carried no lantern. The men shadowing him, their attention taken by the palanquin, would not have marked him.
When he had gone a dozen-odd steps, from behind, at about where the crossroads of Takeyamachi should be, just as he had looked for,
"There!"
came the sound of the palanquin being flung down.
(Done it.)

Toshizō had already passed the crossroads of Nijōhanjiki-chō. By the mistress's reckoning three rōnin had stood at this crossroads, but there was no shadow of them. Lured off by the palanquin, they must have scattered somewhere.
Just then,
(So they've come,)
Toshizō had read it out that far. At once he drew close to the eaves of a house on the south side.
From Takeyamachi came the pattering feet of four or five men running this way. Finding it was a water-cask, they must be turning back.
(It looks as though I may get home safe to Mibu.)
Toshizō made himself thin in the shadow of a latticed bay. So far it had gone just as this man, so skilled in a fight, had read it.
But when that crowd forced its way into the Yoshikago, which stood midway between Takeyamachi and Nijōhanjiki-chō, Toshizō's reckoning went astray.
(This is bad.—)
They had gone in to pick a quarrel, no doubt. A shrill uproar of voices carried all the way here.
Toshizō stepped out into the road.
He started off, meaning to leave the trouble behind him and walk west toward Mibu, but his feet dragged.
(The mistress—it's a pity for her.)
Still, tonight he wanted to get back to the barracks quickly. Everything had grown wearisome. He wanted drink.
Toshizō walked.
He had his guess. That crowd had some tie or other to Osae. Osae had set it up. Even thinking so, Toshizō felt, strangely, neither anger nor fighting spirit.
Know her, and be lost;
know her not, and not lost: the road of love.
(A poor verse, if I say it myself.)
Toshizō looked up at the stars.
He had rounded it off with "the road of love," but Toshizō turned chill wondering whether he had, in fact, ever loved at all.

Women there had been. But he had never done anything that could be called love. Barely, the case of Osae in his memory had resembled it—but resembled it, no more. Only a moment ago it had broken, emptily.
(I seem to be a man with something missing in him.)
Toshizō, to himself, with a resolute face, made a show of contempt.
(This Toshizō will likely, to the end of his days, be a man who can hold no love.)
Even so, let it be, he thought.
(The things ordinary men have—those I will not think about.)
Toshizō walked.
(I am a man cold to women from the first. The women know it. There's no fool who would lose her heart to a man like this.)

But there is the sword. There is the Shinsengumi. In his true feeling for these he yielded to no one. There is Kondō. There is Okita. In his friendship for them he yielded to no one. That was enough. With that alone, might a man not pass a life with some real weight to it?
(Do you see, Toshi?—)
And as he told himself so, Toshizō whirled round.
He crouched down in the road. He loosened his blade in its scabbard.
He had known that four or five sets of feet were coming after him. The master of the Yoshikago, most likely, had confessed.
Five shadows.
Three of them stopped at the crossroads of Nijōhanjiki-chō, and only two came on, unwary.
—This way?
one man said to the other.
—In any case, let's get out to the Muromachi road.
But they had no need to go that far.
For a few steps on, they came upon a man crouched in the road. By the time they marked him they had all but blundered into him.
"Ah!"

The man made to spring back. He raised his right foot and set a hand to his sword-hilt. But in that very posture he went over backward with a cry. Toshizō's Izumi-no-kami Kanesada had leapt up from below and split the man's jaw.
Toshizō rose.
"I am Hijikata Toshizō."

The other man, spared the blade, stood a while with his mouth open, seemingly unable to grasp this reality; then, giving a voice that was no voice, he fled headlong toward the crossroads of Nijōhanjiki-chō.
The three at the crossroads broke into an uproar.
By then Toshizō was no longer in the road. Along the dark eaves of the houses on the north side he was drawing near the crossroads.
—So he was here after all.
There came a rusty voice that seemed to be leading this band.
Toshizō made to spring out. But he clutched at the earth and held himself back.
(Is that not Shichiri Kennosuke?)

It was a start like waking from sleep. He had heard that Shichiri had come up to Kyoto. Not only that: Tōdō Heisuke, too, had seen a man who looked like Shichiri going in and out of the Chōshū residence on Kawaramachi. And in fact Toshizō himself had let one of Shichiri's Hachiōji comrades escape him at Kiyamachi.
"Shichiri."
Toshizō's shadow was spat out from the darkness.
"It's me,"

and by the time he said it, Toshizō was already springing up toward the starry sky. Now there was but a single duelist there. No more sentiment now, no more brooding. His limbs alone leapt. The man beside Shichiri was cut open from the base of the right side of the neck through the shoulder and went down, and leaping over him, the second stroke fell upon Shichiri.
Shichiri, with no time to guard, sprang back to the crossroads lantern and at last drew his blade.
